title: Sodium-Ion Battery Matches Tesla's Quality in Surprise Test, Paving Way for Cheaper EVs
summary: Could the future of electric vehicles be powered by salt? A new study suggests we're closer than ever. Researchers at RWTH Aachen University put a commercial sodium-ion battery from Chinese manufacturer Hina through a gauntlet of tests—and the results caught them off guard. The 120 cells they examined showed remarkable manufacturing uniformity and high-power capability, matching benchmarks set by Tesla's lithium-ion batteries. 'We were positively surprised by how uniform the cells are,' said battery researcher Moritz Schütte. Uniformity is crucial because inconsistent cells degrade faster and pose safety risks. The team used impedance spectroscopy, a non-destructive method, to assess consistency, then subjected the cells to currents ranging from mild to extreme and temperatures from −20°C to 45°C. X-ray imaging and physical disassembly revealed a sophisticated tabless, double-aluminum current collector design—an architecture strikingly similar to Tesla's, which reduces electrical resistance and evens out heat distribution. Sodium is the sixth most abundant element on Earth, found in seawater and soda ash, making it far cheaper and more geopolitically stable than lithium. That could translate to lower-cost batteries for grid storage and commercial vehicles where maximum driving range isn't critical. However, the study also exposed clear weaknesses. Low-temperature charging remains a significant problem; below 0°C, performance drops sharply, requiring thermal management systems. Energy density—how much power fits in a given size—still lags behind top-tier lithium cells. Unexpectedly, the team found high concentrations of unevenly distributed copper in the cathode, raising questions about its role in performance and aging. 'It will be exciting to see future sodium-ion technologies that are free of nickel and copper, as well, while achieving competitive energy density,' Schütte added. The findings, published in Cell Reports Physical Science, mark a milestone: a sodium-ion battery that can stand toe-to-toe with lithium in key metrics. With further refinement, your next electric bus or home battery pack might just run on sodium—and that's no small thing.
why_it_matters: Cheaper, safer batteries could make electric vehicles and renewable energy storage more accessible worldwide, reducing pollution and dependence on scarce resources. The study shows that a technology once dismissed as inferior is now a serious contender, reshaping the industries that today's students may work in or rely on for a clean energy future.

background_read: Lithium-ion batteries dominate electric vehicles and phones today, but lithium is scarce, environmentally damaging to mine, and concentrated in just a few countries. Sodium, by contrast, is the sixth most abundant element on Earth—the main ingredient in table salt—and can be extracted from seawater.

In the past decade, sodium-ion battery research intensified, especially in China, where companies like Hina aim to mass-produce them for grid storage and affordable electric vehicles. Sodium-ion is seen as a cheaper, geopolitically stable alternative.

Tesla's 2020 Battery Day unveiled a 'tabless' 4680 cell design that lowers internal resistance and heat, setting a high benchmark for manufacturing quality and consistency. Matching that benchmark with sodium-ion chemistry was unexpected.

RWTH Aachen University, a top German engineering school, performed the testing and published the results in July 2025. The findings mark a milestone where sodium-ion not only works but can rival top lithium cells in several critical manufacturing and performance measures.

perspectives.description: Advocates celebrate sodium-ion as a democratizer: using abundant salt-derived materials avoids the ethical, environmental, and supply-chain problems of lithium and cobalt. Mass adoption could bring clean electric transport and power backup to developing nations at lower cost.

Critics highlight that sodium-ion still can't match lithium in energy density, meaning bulkier batteries and less range for passenger cars. The poor low-temperature charging also demands extra thermal management systems, adding cost and complexity.

Analysts point out that battery chemistries rarely replace each other overnight; instead, they partition into niches. Sodium-ion may dominate grid storage and commercial fleets while lithium-ion remains in premium EVs—similar to how gasoline, diesel, and electric motors serve different transport roles.

If researchers eliminate nickel and copper from the cathode, as the study's author hinted, costs could drop further and environmental impacts shrink. The next hurdle is scaling up factories and proving long-term reliability, a challenge requiring both engineering breakthroughs and government incentives to build a new supply chain.
